prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the improper joinder doctrine requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. The removing defendants must show there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against the in-state defendant.

Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, and the removal statute is strictly construed against removal. Any doubt is resolved in favor of remand. *See Gasch v. Hartford Accident & Indem. Co.*, 491 F.3d 278, 281–82 (5th Cir. 2007). The party invoking federal jurisdiction through removal bears the burden of establishing it. That burden includes showing that the non-diverse defendant was improperly joined. *See Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011).

The en banc Fifth Circuit has settled the standard. A removing party may establish improper joinder in one of two ways: by showing actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, or by showing that the plaintiff is unable to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse defendant. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 573 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc). Only the second is at issue here. Under that prong, the test is "whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Id.*; *accord Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003). The Fifth Circuit has also adopted "improper joinder" as the preferred label for this doctrine. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 571 n.1; *see also Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200 (5th Cir. 2016).

The burden is a heavy one. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005); *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249. The court must evaluate all factual allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. It must resolve all contested issues of substantive fact and all ambiguities in the controlling state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249. The removing party therefore cannot prevail by showing that the plaintiff's claim is weak, or that it will probably fail on the merits. It must show that the claim has no reasonable basis at all.

The "reasonable basis" requirement does ask for more than a purely theoretical possibility of recovery. *Griggs v. State Farm Lloyds*, 181 F.3d 694, 699–701 (5th Cir. 1999). That qualification does not shift the burden. It describes what the plaintiff's claim must be, a reasonable possibility rather than a speculative one. It does not require the plaintiff to prove the claim at the jurisdictional stage. The defendant must still demonstrate that no reasonable possibility exists.

### II. The inquiry is a limited, Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, not a merits adjudication.

The ordinary method is to "conduct a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, looking initially at the allegations of the complaint to determine whether the complaint states a claim under state law against the in-state defendant." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. If the complaint states a claim, there is ordinarily no improper joinder and the inquiry ends. *Id.* Applying that analysis, the Fifth Circuit has held that the federal pleading standard governs whether the complaint states a claim against the non-diverse defendant. *Int'l Energy Ventures*, 818 F.3d at 208.

A court may "pierce the pleadings" only in a narrow category of cases. These are cases in which the plaintiff has "misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. Even then, the court's inquiry is limited. It may not become a summary trial on the merits. *Id.* at 573–74; *Hart v. Bayer Corp.*, 199 F.3d 239, 246–47 (5th Cir. 2000). The Fifth Circuit has cautioned that a court should not use a motion to remand to decide the merits of the claim against the in-state defendant. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 574. Doing so would deprive the plaintiff of a state forum on the strength of a preliminary assessment of the merits.

### III. Defendants cannot carry their burden here.

Plaintiff's [Petition/Complaint] alleges [describe the specific facts and the state-law cause of action asserted against the in-state defendant]. (ROA.[__].) Those allegations, taken as true and viewed in Plaintiff's favor, state a claim under [State] law against [In-State Defendant]. Defendants' contrary arguments depend on disputed facts [or on an unsettled question of state law]. The standard requires the court to resolve those matters in Plaintiff's favor. *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249. Defendants have not shown that [State] law forecloses recovery. At most, they have argued that Plaintiff may ultimately lose, which is not the test. *See Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573–74.

Because Defendants have not shown that there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against [In-State Defendant], that defendant was not improperly joined. Complete diversity is lacking, and the district court's judgment should be [reversed/vacated] with instructions to remand to state court.
